The Hall-Mills Case. In September 1922, the bodies of Reverend Edward Hall and his lover Eleanor Mills, a choir singer, were found murdered on a rural road in New Jersey. Hall's wife, Frances Hall, and her brothers were tried for the crime. Circumstantial evidence and witness inconsistencies made the trial sensational but inconclusive, and though they were acquitted, the case remained controversial, epitomizing 1920s anxieties over sexuality, respectability, and justice.

Reverend Edward Hall was a prominent Protestant minister. Eleanor Mills was a thirty-four-year-old choir singer and mother of two. Both were found shot and stabbed to death on September 16, 1922, in De Russey's Lane near New Brunswick, New Jersey. Hall had been having an affair with Mills, and both were married to other people. The murders occurred in a pastoral setting, initially suggesting a crime of passion rooted in moral transgression.

Frances Hall, Edward's wife, quickly came under suspicion. She claimed ignorance but was widely believed to have orchestrated or participated in the murders out of sexual jealousy and wounded pride. Frances's two brothers, Willie Stevens and Henry Stevens, were also tried. Willie was simple-minded, and the prosecution suggested Frances and Henry were co-conspirators.

The trial came in 1926 and featured conflicting eyewitness testimony, disputed timelines, and limited physical evidence. The defense exploited weaknesses in the state's case and raised questions about Frances's mental state. All three defendants were acquitted in December 1926, but the verdict left the public deeply skeptical, as circumstantial evidence suggested guilt but fell short of legal proof.

The case became emblematic of class privilege's power in the justice system. Frances Hall's social standing, the ambiguity of evidence, and the defense's courtroom skill combined to evade conviction despite widespread belief in her involvement.
